FY2025 (the first full calendar year as a public company) delivered $5.1 billion in revenue (+168 per cent from $1.9B in FY2024 and $229M in FY2023), Q4 2025 revenue of $1.6 billion, and a net loss of $1.2 billion. The forward visibility is extraordinary: $60.7 billion of Remaining Performance Obligations at year-end 2025 (up from $15.1B at year-end 2024) on a weighted-average contract duration of approximately 5 years. The 2,189 employees (1,967 US, 222 across 19 other countries) build and operate the GPU clusters under multi-year facility leases and a complex senior-notes-plus-convertibles-plus-asset-level-debt capital structure. The investment proposition compresses AI capex sustainability, Microsoft concentration risk, the Magnetar overhang, Nvidia GPU allocation continuity, and the operating leverage potential as the 5-year contracted RPO converts to recognised revenue against a substantially built-up fixed-cost base.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
On March 28, 2025, CoreWeave, Inc. began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker CRWV after pricing 37.5 million shares at $40 each. The final prospectus showed that 36.59 million shares were sold by the company and 910,000 by selling stockholders, implying roughly $1.46 billion of gross primary proceeds and $36.4 million of gross selling-stockholder proceeds; the 2025 annual report later recorded approximately $1.4 billion of net proceeds to the company after underwriting discounts and commissions. At the offer price, the deal implied an equity value of roughly $23 billion. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm)

## Atlantic Crypto to AI Infrastructure

The company that came public in 2025 had been formed in September 2017 as The Atlantic Crypto Corporation LLC, converted into a Delaware corporation as Atlantic Crypto Corporation in September 2018, and renamed CoreWeave, Inc. in December 2019. What began as GPU-heavy crypto infrastructure was redirected into AI cloud computing as demand for machine-learning capacity accelerated; by 2025, the company said annual revenue had reached $5.1 billion. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm)

## The Revenue Trajectory

CoreWeave's growth curve is, by any ordinary standard, extraordinary.

| Year | Revenue (USD) | YoY Growth |
|------|--------------|------------|
| 2022 | $16M | — |
| 2023 | $229M | ~14× |
| 2024 | $1.915B | ~8× |
| 2025 | $5.131B | ~168% |

The 2025 total was built quarter by quarter: $981.6 million in the first quarter, $1.21 billion in the second, $1.36 billion in the third and $1.57 billion in the fourth. In its February 26, 2026 results release, CoreWeave said it had become "the fastest cloud in history to reach $5 billion in annual revenue" — a bold line, but one that matched the reported trajectory. [CoreWeave Q1 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Q2 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Second-Quarter-2025-Results/) [CoreWeave Q3 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Third-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave FY2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx)

## Customer Concentration and the Microsoft Anchor

Customer concentration remained the defining risk. The March 2025 S-1 said Microsoft represented 62 percent of 2024 revenue, up from 35 percent in 2023; the 2025 10-K later said Microsoft accounted for approximately 67 percent of 2025 revenue, while the top two customers had represented 77 percent of 2024 revenue. The first-quarter 2026 10-Q showed that the top two customers still made up 65 percent of quarterly revenue. [CoreWeave S-1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525044231/d899798ds1.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000222/crwv-20260331.htm)

Diversification nevertheless moved from narrative to signed contracts. CoreWeave said in September 2025 that its expanded OpenAI relationship had taken total announced OpenAI commitments to roughly $22.4 billion; it said the same quarter that Meta had signed an initial deal worth up to about $14.2 billion, and in April 2026 Meta expanded that commitment to about $21 billion through December 2032. In the April 2026 shareholder letter, Michael Intrator said no single customer represented more than 35 percent of revenue backlog, against 85 percent at the start of 2025. [CoreWeave OpenAI expansion](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Expands-Agreement-with-OpenAI-by-up-to-6-5B/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Q3 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Third-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Meta expansion](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-and-Meta-Announce-21-Billion-Expanded-AI-Infrastructure-Agreement/default.aspx) [CoreWeave 2025 shareholder letter](https://www.coreweave.com/news/ceo-michael-intrators-2025-letter-to-shareholders)

## Nvidia: Supplier, Investor, Backstop

Central to CoreWeave's competitive position was its relationship with Nvidia: a hardware supplier, a pre-IPO strategic investor and, through the arrangements described in the prospectus, part of the demand-and-supply architecture that underwrote fleet expansion. By the April 22, 2026 proxy, Nvidia beneficially owned 47.2 million Class A shares, equal to 10.7 percent of the economic interest and 3.3 percent of the voting power. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm)

## Capital Structure and the RPO Runway

The cost of that growth was visible in the balance sheet. At December 31, 2025, CoreWeave reported $21.615 billion of debt principal outstanding, or $21.373 billion net of discounts and issuance costs; interest expense of $1.229 billion helped produce a $1.167 billion net loss even though operating loss was only $46 million. Cash paid for property and equipment reached $10.3 billion in 2025, and net cash used in investing activities was $7.7 billion in the first quarter of 2026 alone. [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000222/crwv-20260331.htm)

Against that capital intensity sat an order book that kept getting bigger. The audited 10-K reported remaining performance obligations of $60.7 billion at December 31, 2025, up from $15.1 billion a year earlier, with weighted-average contract duration of about five years. Management's February 2026 earnings release used the broader "revenue backlog" measure and put that figure at $66.8 billion at year-end 2025; by May 7, 2026 the company said revenue backlog had risen to $99.4 billion, active power had surpassed 1 GW and contracted power had climbed above 3.5 GW. [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave FY2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Q1 2026 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2026-Results/default.aspx)

| Date | Backlog disclosure |
|------|--------------------|
| Dec. 31, 2024 | $15.1B RPO |
| Mar. 31, 2025 | $25.9B revenue backlog |
| Jun. 30, 2025 | $30.1B revenue backlog |
| Sep. 30, 2025 | $55.6B revenue backlog |
| Dec. 31, 2025 | $60.7B RPO / $66.8B revenue backlog |
| Mar. 31, 2026 | $99.4B revenue backlog |

## The Central Question

By the freeze date, CoreWeave had become the clearest public-market test of whether contracted AI infrastructure demand could outrun the financing burden required to serve it. The central questions were no longer whether demand existed; they were whether Microsoft concentration would fade fast enough, whether backlog would convert without destroying cash flow, and whether a GPU-backed balance sheet could remain an advantage once the hyperscalers' own fleets caught up.

chapters.title: From 2017 Ethereum mining to the March 2025 AI infrastructure IPO
chapters.body:
The founding of The Atlantic Crypto Corporation LLC in September 2017 did not announce itself as a turning point in American AI infrastructure. Michael Intrator, Brian Venturo, and Brannin McBee used a Delaware vehicle to mine Ethereum with GPU clusters, applying the electricity-arbitrage and asset-discipline instincts they had developed at Hudson Ridge Asset Management to a new asset class. What distinguished the venture from the broader crypto-mining wave was not rhetoric but operations: the founders built data-center capacity, ran GPU fleets at scale, and learned the thermal, power and procurement disciplines that later underpinned CoreWeave's AI cloud. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm)

## Origins in Ethereum Mining

Atlantic Crypto was born at a moment when Ethereum mining required exactly the hardware that the AI industry would later consume in enormous volume: high-end Nvidia GPUs, housed in purpose-built facilities, drawing significant power loads and demanding careful thermal management. The co-founders brought to this problem the capital-intensity discipline of natural gas trading, where managing large physical positions against volatile commodity prices had been their professional formation.

The period from 2017 through roughly 2019 was primarily operational in character. Atlantic Crypto built out GPU clusters for proof-of-work mining, confronted the engineering challenges of fleet management at real scale, and accumulated data-centre and infrastructure expertise that would prove transferable in ways the founders may not yet have fully articulated. The crypto mining cycle provided both the hardware and the operational knowledge; it also compressed what might otherwise have been years of learning into a narrow window of intense, capital-hungry execution. When the cryptocurrency mining cycle eventually moderated, the institutional memory of running thousands of GPUs in production — thermal discipline, power procurement, cluster orchestration — proved to be the durable asset.

## The Pivot and the Rebrand

As the mining cycle softened, the founders redirected the hardware base toward AI and high-performance compute. The legal entity converted into Atlantic Crypto Corporation in September 2018, changed its name to CoreWeave, Inc. in December 2019, and said in the 2025 annual report that it launched the CoreWeave Cloud Platform in 2020. The strategic pivot was straightforward: enterprise customers needed dense Nvidia GPU capacity faster than the general-purpose clouds could supply it, and CoreWeave already understood how to procure, rack and operate that hardware at scale. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm)

The pivot preserved the core operational asset — the people, the data-centre facilities, the GPU procurement relationships, the cluster-operations expertise — while replacing the mining workload with cloud compute customers. It was, in the financial vocabulary CoreWeave would later deploy for investors, a high-leverage transition: the fixed-cost infrastructure was substantially in place, and the new revenue model could run on the same asset base with markedly better unit economics than proof-of-work mining had ever offered. Early Microsoft engagement — the relationship that would later define CoreWeave's revenue profile at scale — dates to this transitional period, as hyperscalers began exploring external GPU cloud capacity to supplement internal build.

## Building at Hyperscale, 2022–2024

The financial trajectory in the three years following the pivot is among the more striking in recent technology history. Revenue grew from approximately $16 million in 2022 to $228 million in 2023, and then to approximately $1.9 billion in 2024 — a compound growth rate that reflected both the velocity of AI investment following the November 2022 release of ChatGPT and CoreWeave's specific positioning as a preferred external GPU cloud for the largest AI workloads.

The Microsoft anchor relationship became, by 2024, the dominant feature of CoreWeave's revenue profile, with approximately 62 percent of fiscal 2024 revenue deriving from a single customer — a concentration level that would become the single most-debated investor concern. The scale of the relationship was partially quantified through CoreWeave's remaining performance obligations: the company reported $15.1 billion of RPO at the end of 2024, representing signed customer commitments not yet recognised as revenue and giving institutional investors a multi-year forward revenue runway to underwrite. [CoreWeave S-1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525044231/d899798ds1.htm)

The Nvidia relationship evolved through the same period from supplier to something considerably more layered. Nvidia held approximately a 6 percent pre-IPO equity stake in CoreWeave, and the two companies entered a backstop purchase agreement under which Nvidia could, in certain circumstances, absorb GPU capacity that CoreWeave had procured — an arrangement that effectively positioned Nvidia as a customer of last resort and gave CoreWeave's procurement model a degree of downside protection unusual in cloud infrastructure. The equity investment formalised what had been a strategically important supplier relationship; CoreWeave's preferential access to Nvidia's latest GPU generations — the H100, H200, and GB200 architectures — was widely regarded by analysts as a meaningful competitive differentiator against both hyperscalers and specialist rivals.

The capital structure supporting this growth was equally unconventional. CoreWeave announced a $50 million Magnetar investment in November 2021, then raised a $2.3 billion debt facility led by Magnetar and Blackstone in August 2023, followed by a $1.1 billion Series C and a $7.5 billion debt facility in May 2024. By the 2026 proxy, Magnetar remained the largest financial holder disclosed outside the founders, with 77.7 million Class A shares, equal to 17.1 percent of the economic interest and 5.3 percent of the voting power. [CoreWeave Magnetar financing](https://www.coreweave.com/blog/coreweave-specialized-cloud-provider-raises-50-million-in-new-capital-from-magnetar) [CoreWeave $2.3B debt facility](https://www.coreweave.com/news/coreweave-secures-2-3-billion-debt-financing-facility-led-by-magnetar-capital-and-blackstone-to-meet-surging-demand-and-ongoing-expansion-of-specialized-cloud-infrastructure-to-power-ai) [CoreWeave Series C](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2024/CoreWeave-Secures-1-1-Billion-in-Series-C-Funding-to-Drive-the-Next-Generation-of-Cloud-Computing-for-the-Future-of-AI/default.aspx) [CoreWeave $7.5B debt facility](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2024/CoreWeave-Secures-7-5-Billion-Debt-Financing-Facility-led-by-Blackstone-and-Magnetar/default.aspx) [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm)

## The March 2025 IPO

The IPO priced at $40 per share on March 27, 2025 and began trading the following morning, below the indicated range of $47 to $55. The final prospectus showed 37.5 million shares sold, of which 36.59 million were primary and 910,000 secondary; the 2025 annual report later disclosed an additional 1.76 million-share partial over-allotment exercise in April 2025 that generated a further $68 million of net proceeds to the company. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm)

The distance between a New Jersey cryptocurrency mining operation and a $23 billion NASDAQ-listed AI cloud was, by March 2025, approximately eight years of GPU operational discipline, two debt-market innovations, one strategic Nvidia alliance, and a revenue ramp that most technology analysts had not modelled as achievable on the timescale CoreWeave actually executed it.

chapters.title: GPU cloud product, customer engagement model, and data centre footprint
chapters.body:
## A Purpose-Built Stack for AI Compute

CoreWeave built its GPU cloud product around a single organizing principle: that the workloads propelling the artificial intelligence cycle — frontier-model training runs, high-throughput inference serving, reinforcement learning pipelines — demanded infrastructure engineered specifically for those tasks, not the general-purpose compute architectures that Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud had assembled over the preceding two decades for transactional databases and web applications.

The product catalogue centred on Nvidia's highest-capability data-center GPU generations, but the company's own disclosures described the stack more in operational than component-detail terms. The prospectus and annual report positioned CoreWeave as a preferred large-scale operator of H100-, H200- and Blackwell-era systems, while the platform and AI data-centers pages emphasized dense GPU clusters, high-performance interconnect, and software tuned specifically for training and inference workloads at scale. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave platform](https://www.coreweave.com/platform) [CoreWeave AI data centers](https://www.coreweave.com/ai-infrastructure)

| GPU generation family | CoreWeave disclosure context |
|---|---|
| H100 | Core training fleet through the 2024 buildout |
| H200 | Later Hopper-generation expansion |
| GB200 / Blackwell-era systems | Early next-generation deployments and first-to-market positioning |

Alongside the GPU instance offerings, CoreWeave built a Kubernetes-based orchestration layer that handled GPU scheduling, workload management, and multi-tenant resource allocation across its data-centre footprint. The Kubernetes foundation allowed customers to run containerized AI training and inference workloads without managing the underlying GPU cluster configuration directly. For high-performance computing customers with existing Slurm-based job scheduling workflows — common in research and enterprise environments that adopted GPU compute before the generative AI cycle — CoreWeave offered compatible interfaces alongside its primary Kubernetes API surface.

## The Customer Engagement Model: Reserved Capacity at Scale

CoreWeave's commercial architecture diverged from the on-demand, pay-per-use model that the major public cloud providers used as the standard enterprise entry point. The company's primary revenue mechanism was the multi-year reserved-capacity contract: a customer committed to a specified quantum of GPU compute for a defined term — typically measured in years rather than months — in exchange for price certainty and guaranteed allocation. The structure transferred capacity risk to the customer and allowed CoreWeave to finance GPU procurement against contracted future revenue.

The model's logic was straightforward for both sides. For AI laboratories and large enterprise customers, guaranteed GPU access at scale was worth more than on-demand flexibility: the scarcity of Nvidia H100 and H200 GPU capacity through 2023 and 2024 meant that customers unable to secure committed allocations faced multi-month lead times on the spot market. For CoreWeave, multi-year committed revenue underpinned the leverage it needed to finance GPU procurement — requiring billions of dollars deployed ahead of any revenue recognition — against term-loan facilities collateralized by the GPU hardware itself.

The financial outcome of that model was visible in the company's $15.1 billion remaining performance obligations at end-2024 — a contracted revenue runway that formed the central investment case for institutional buyers approaching the March 2025 IPO.

Microsoft's willingness to commit multi-year GPU capacity spend to CoreWeave — rather than routing all AI compute demand through Azure — signalled the limits of hyperscaler in-house GPU capacity at the pace the AI demand cycle required.

OpenAI entered CoreWeave's formal contract stack in March 2025, when the company announced an initial agreement worth up to $11.9 billion; CoreWeave then disclosed a further $4 billion expansion in May 2025 and a new agreement worth up to $6.5 billion in September 2025, saying total announced OpenAI commitments had reached approximately $22.4 billion. The relationship reflected OpenAI's decision to diversify GPU supply beyond a single infrastructure channel and gave CoreWeave a second marquee anchor alongside Microsoft. [CoreWeave Q1 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Q2 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Second-Quarter-2025-Results/) [CoreWeave OpenAI expansion](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Expands-Agreement-with-OpenAI-by-up-to-6-5B/default.aspx)

## Data-Centre Footprint and Capacity Expansion

CoreWeave's data-center footprint expanded rapidly to absorb the GPU procurement commitments it was making against contracted customer demand. The 10-K said the company was headquartered in Livingston, New Jersey and leased data-center space in the United States, the United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden and Norway; the prospectus had also described contracted capacity in Canada and a European presence established in London, Barcelona and Falun by the end of 2024. By December 31, 2025, CoreWeave reported 43 data centers with more than 850 MW of active power and approximately 3.1 GW of contracted power capacity, and by the May 7, 2026 results release it said active power had surpassed 1 GW and contracted power had risen above 3.5 GW. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave Q1 2026 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2026-Results/default.aspx)

The density of GPU deployment within each facility substantially exceeded that of general-purpose cloud data centres. Nvidia H100 and H200 SXM5 configurations in high-performance AI clusters demanded significantly higher power draw per rack than conventional server deployments, and the cooling infrastructure requirements — air cooling for earlier-generation systems, with liquid cooling increasingly dominant for GB200 NVL72 racks — represented a material component of the data-centre capital expenditure alongside the GPU hardware itself.

## GPU Procurement and the Nvidia Strategic Relationship

The supply-chain dynamic for Nvidia H100, H200, and GB200 GPUs through 2023 and 2024 was characterized by demand that substantially exceeded manufacturing output, with allocation decisions made by Nvidia on a customer-by-customer basis. CoreWeave's ability to secure large GPU allocations ahead of the broader market — enabling eight-fold revenue growth from 2023 to 2024 — was a function of its position as one of Nvidia's largest and most strategically aligned customers.

Nvidia's approximately six percent pre-IPO equity stake and its backstop purchase agreement (detailed in the Snapshot chapter) reduced CoreWeave's residual capacity risk and signalled Nvidia's strategic commitment to the model.

The term-loan financing structure CoreWeave employed to fund GPU purchases used the hardware itself as collateral — a model that specialized lenders had developed for the GPU cloud sector and that allowed CoreWeave to finance GPU acquisitions with substantial leverage. The resulting capital structure carried significant debt load, and the company's free cash flow profile through the high-growth phase was materially negative as GPU procurement commitments outpaced revenue recognition on new contracts.

By the March 2025 IPO, the company had built a purpose-built AI GPU cloud operating at a scale no pure-play competitor had achieved — narrower than any hyperscaler's catalogue, but arguably deeper in the specific engineering domain that the AI compute cycle had made the most valuable compute capability in the technology industry.

chapters.title: $1.9B revenue, $15.1B RPO, and the GPU capex intensity question
chapters.body:
## The Numbers That Defined the Offering

The $15.1 billion remaining performance obligations at year-end 2024 — approximately eight times the company's annual revenue run-rate — requires careful parsing. RPO under US GAAP accounting standards represents the transaction price allocated to unsatisfied or partially unsatisfied performance commitments under existing contracts. In CoreWeave's business model, these are principally multi-year GPU cloud reservation agreements with enterprise customers committing to minimum capacity purchases across defined contract periods.

The $15.1 billion figure at end-2024 therefore represented not a forecast, not a pipeline, but a contractual obligation that customers had already signed. Converting that stock of contracted revenue into recognised revenue would, by construction, require nothing more from the sales organisation — only operational delivery of the committed compute capacity.

## The Microsoft Dependency

Microsoft's 62 percent share of 2024 revenue — roughly $1.19 billion — made CoreWeave one of Microsoft's larger compute vendors. The strategic logic: Azure, operationally constrained by its own data-centre buildout timelines while serving OpenAI, needed external H100 capacity with shorter lead times. The IPO pricing at $40 (below the indicated $47-to-$55 range) partially reflected investor concern about this concentration.

The dependency carried obvious risk. A single customer accounting for 62 percent of revenue meant that any material change in Microsoft's procurement strategy, contract renegotiation, or competitive substitution would immediately restructure CoreWeave's revenue profile. The post-IPO market-cap entry point of approximately $23 billion implied a forward revenue multiple that assumed meaningful diversification of the customer base over the contract period.

The diversification thesis rested on the $15.1 billion RPO: if a meaningful share derived from customers other than Microsoft, concentration would decline mechanically as contracts converted. The formal OpenAI contracts arrived only after the IPO filing window — first in March 2025, then through expansions in May and September 2025 — and by early 2026 the diversification case rested not on aspiration alone but on signed commitments from OpenAI, Meta, Jane Street and Anthropic. [CoreWeave Q1 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave OpenAI expansion](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Expands-Agreement-with-OpenAI-by-up-to-6-5B/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Meta expansion](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-and-Meta-Announce-21-Billion-Expanded-AI-Infrastructure-Agreement/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Anthropic agreement](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Announces-Multi-Year-Agreement-With-Anthropic/default.aspx) [Jane Street agreement](https://www.coreweave.com/news/jane-street-signs-6-billion-ai-cloud-agreement-with-coreweave)

## Capital Structure and the GPU Collateral Machine

The financial model that produced $1.915 billion in revenue was built on a capex intensity that had no close analogue in conventional cloud or SaaS comparables. CoreWeave's primary capital expenditure was GPU procurement — principally Nvidia H100, H200, and GB200 systems — plus the data centre colocation and power infrastructure required to operate them at the density that AI training workloads demand.

CoreWeave financed the gap between capital outlay and revenue recognition through debt secured against GPU assets. The prospectus said the company had secured cumulative DDTL commitments of $9.9 billion by December 31, 2024; the 2025 annual report showed how quickly that stack expanded, with debt principal reaching $21.615 billion by year-end 2025. The model preserved growth but left operating results highly sensitive to financing cost and asset utilization. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm)

The interest cost was not the only pressure on margins. GPU depreciation — the accounting recognition of the capital cost of the H100 and successor systems over their operational lives — flowed through cost of revenue, structurally elevating cost of goods sold relative to software-as-a-service comparables. CoreWeave was, at its financial core, a highly leveraged GPU rental operation: it bought hardware at high prices, depreciated it rapidly, serviced substantial debt against it, and priced customer contracts at rates sufficient to clear all those costs plus a return on equity.

## Free Cash Flow and the Conversion Question

The free cash flow implications of that capital structure were severe during the buildout phase. CoreWeave's operating cash generation was partially offset by the continuing capital requirements of expanding the GPU fleet to meet the demand implicit in the $15.1 billion RPO. The company was in a structural position common to rapidly growing infrastructure businesses: the contractual commitments that represented the strongest evidence of future revenue also required accelerating capital deployment to fulfill.

The investor framework for evaluating CoreWeave's financial profile therefore rested not on near-term free cash flow generation but on the RPO conversion dynamic. If the $15.1 billion in contracted obligations converted to revenue at the rates implied by the contract tenor — and if the marginal capex required to serve that contracted base was lower than the capex required to win it — the business would generate substantial free cash flow during the back half of the contract period.

Post-IPO quarterly filings began to provide evidence for that conversion. Revenue in the first quarter of 2025 reached approximately $981.6 million — more than half of the full-year 2024 figure in a single quarter. The annualised run-rate implied by Q1 2025 performance placed 2025 full-year revenue trajectory well above the $1.915 billion 2024 baseline.

## The Nvidia Dimension

Nvidia's approximately six percent pre-IPO equity stake, supplier role, and backstop purchase agreement created a triangulation of interests without precedent in the cloud infrastructure market. The procurement advantage this relationship conferred — access to H100 and H200 systems at scale, ahead of competing buyers — was the operational foundation of the $15.1 billion RPO. For investors evaluating competitive durability, the Nvidia dimension was a structural pillar, not a footnote.

chapters.title: Pre-IPO trajectory through the March 2025 listing and post-IPO quarters
chapters.body:
## The Numbers Behind the Listing

When CoreWeave filed its S-1 registration statement in March 2025, the headline figures drove the road-show conversation: $1.915 billion of 2024 revenue, up from $229 million in 2023 and $16 million in 2022, and $15.1 billion of remaining performance obligations at year-end 2024. The filing also showed how much physical infrastructure sat beneath those numbers: 32 data centers and roughly 360 MW of active power at December 31, 2024. [CoreWeave S-1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525044231/d899798ds1.htm) [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm)

## Customer Concentration and the Microsoft Question

The road show became an extended discussion of whether Microsoft's 62 percent revenue share was a feature or a defect. CoreWeave's answer was that Microsoft's multi-year contracted spend was precisely the durable demand signal that justified the capital intensity. Investors who came later to the name, and particularly public-equity investors who had not funded the private rounds, saw the same fact as the principal risk. The debate did not disappear after listing: the 2025 annual report showed Microsoft still accounted for approximately 67 percent of 2025 revenue, even as the company argued that backlog diversification was improving quickly. [CoreWeave S-1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525044231/d899798ds1.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 shareholder letter](https://www.coreweave.com/news/ceo-michael-intrators-2025-letter-to-shareholders)

## IPO Pricing and Structure

The March 27, 2025 pricing at $40 per share — below the indicated $47-to-$55 range — was a direct expression of the discount public investors demanded for customer concentration and hardware-backed leverage. The final prospectus showed 37.5 million shares sold in the deal: 36.59 million primary shares from the company and 910,000 shares from selling stockholders. That meant gross primary proceeds of roughly $1.46 billion and gross selling-stockholder proceeds of only about $36.4 million, not the much larger secondary take that early summaries often implied. The 2025 annual report later said the company received about $1.4 billion of net IPO proceeds and a further $68 million when the underwriters partially exercised their over-allotment option in April 2025. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm)

## Capex Intensity and the Debt Architecture

CoreWeave's capital intensity was among the highest in the sector because the business required hardware to be bought and commissioned before revenue could be recognized. At the time of the prospectus, the company had already assembled cumulative DDTL commitments of $9.9 billion. That financing stack did not stop growing after the IPO: debt principal reached $21.615 billion by December 31, 2025, the company closed an $8.5 billion investment-grade-rated GPU-backed facility in March 2026, and on May 18, 2026 it announced a further $3.1 billion DDTL 5.0 facility tied to public-market execution. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave $8.5B financing](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Closes-Landmark-8-5-Billion-Financing-Facility-Achieving-First-Investment-Grade-Rated-GPU-backed-Financing/default.aspx) [CoreWeave $3.1B financing](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Closes-3-1-Billion-Loan-Facility-Expanding-Access-to-Public-Markets-for-GPU-backed-Financing/default.aspx)

## The First Reporting Cycle as a Public Company

The post-IPO reporting cycle arrived quickly and, through the freeze date, broadly reinforced the demand thesis. Revenue rose to $981.6 million in the first quarter of 2025, $1.21 billion in the second, $1.36 billion in the third and $1.57 billion in the fourth; revenue backlog moved from $25.9 billion at March 31, 2025 to $30.1 billion at June 30, $55.6 billion at September 30 and $66.8 billion at December 31. By May 7, 2026, CoreWeave reported first-quarter revenue of $2.078 billion and revenue backlog of $99.4 billion. The IPO was therefore not the end of the story but the point at which the company began proving, quarter by quarter, that the contract machine and the capital machine could keep pace with one another. [CoreWeave Q1 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Q2 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Second-Quarter-2025-Results/) [CoreWeave Q3 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Third-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave FY2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Q1 2026 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2026-Results/default.aspx)

chapters.title: Intrator, Venturo, McBee, Salanki CFO, and the post-IPO board
chapters.body:
## The Commodities Traders Who Built a GPU Cloud

Few origin stories in American technology were as improbable as CoreWeave's. Michael Intrator, Brian Venturo and Brannin McBee came to GPUs from natural-gas and environmental-markets trading, not from software. The prospectus and proxy make clear how fully that background shaped the company: Intrator had worked at Natsource Asset Management and later co-founded Hudson Ridge; Venturo had also come through Hudson Ridge and Natsource; McBee's remit developed into capital formation and business development rather than product management in the conventional software sense. The founding instinct was to treat compute capacity as a capital-intensive physical asset and to finance it against contracted demand. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm)

Intrator's biography helps explain the tone of the company. The prospectus said he had served as Chief Executive Officer, President and Chair since September 2017, after work at Natsource and Hudson Ridge, and held degrees from Binghamton University and Columbia's School of International and Public Affairs. That is not the standard resume of a public-cloud chief executive, but it fits CoreWeave's unusual combination of commodities logic, hardware procurement and capital-markets engineering. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm)

## Venturo, McBee, Salanki and the Operating Core

The co-founder operating model remained intact through the freeze date, but the roles were more clearly delineated than some outside summaries suggested. The proxy said Venturo had served as a director since April 2019 and as Chief Strategy Officer since March 2024, after serving as Chief Technology Officer from October 2017 through March 2024. McBee was listed as Chief Development Officer, having served as Chief Strategy Officer from September 2017 through March 2024. Peter Salanki, not Nitin Agrawal, was the technical co-founder in the current operating structure: the prospectus said Salanki became Chief Technology Officer in March 2024 after serving as Vice President of Engineering and then Director of Engineering. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm)

The distinction mattered because it separated technology, commercial strategy and capital formation into three explicit domains. Venturo ran strategy and major customer relationships; McBee ran development, financing architecture and partnership structures; Salanki owned the engineering stack that had to make those commitments deliverable in production. That division was more precise than the shorthand often used around the company during its IPO.

## Agrawal and the Professional-Management Layer

The professional-management layer that surrounded the founders was assembled quickly ahead of the listing. The proxy said Nitin Agrawal had served as Chief Financial Officer since March 2024 and as Treasurer since June 2025. Sachin Jain had served as Chief Operating Officer since August 2024. Chen Goldberg joined as Senior Vice President of Engineering in August 2024 and became Executive Vice President, Product and Engineering in February 2026. Michelle O'Rourke was appointed Chief People Officer on October 18, 2024, moving up from Senior Director of Human Resources. [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm) [CoreWeave Michelle O'Rourke appointment](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2024/CoreWeave-Announces-Appointment-of-Michelle-ORourke-as-Chief-People-Officer/default.aspx)

That hiring cadence was not cosmetic. It reflected the reality that a company generating $1.915 billion of revenue in 2024 and carrying a complex hardware-backed financing stack could not enter the public markets with only a founder bench. The company still presented itself as founder-led, but it no longer operated like a garage-scale specialty cloud.

## The Post-IPO Board: Founders, Independence and Capital

The board composition at the freeze date also looked different from some IPO-era descriptions. As of the April 22, 2026 proxy, the six directors were Michael Intrator, Brian Venturo, Karen Boone, Glenn Hutchins, Margaret C. Whitman and Jack Cogen. McBee was not listed as a director. Boone had joined the board in January 2025, Hutchins in February 2025 and Whitman in March 2025. The proxy also said Hutchins had been appointed Lead Independent Director in March 2025 and reappointed in March 2026. [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm)

The board had also already begun to evolve. On April 16, 2026, Jack Cogen notified the board that he would not stand for re-election at the June 2026 annual meeting, though he remained a director through the end of his term. That detail mattered because it underscored that the governance structure was not frozen at IPO. [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm)

## Key Institutional Holders

The ownership picture had moved on from the rough IPO-era shorthand of "Magnetar at 30 percent" and "Nvidia at 6 percent". The 2026 proxy said Magnetar beneficially owned 77.7 million Class A shares, equal to 17.1 percent of the economic interest and 5.3 percent of the voting power. Nvidia beneficially owned 47.2 million Class A shares, equal to 10.7 percent of the economic interest and 3.3 percent of the voting power. Jane Street, following its April 2026 investment, was disclosed with 28.9 million Class A shares, or 6.5 percent of the economic interest and 2.0 percent of the voting power. [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm) [Jane Street agreement](https://www.coreweave.com/news/jane-street-signs-6-billion-ai-cloud-agreement-with-coreweave)

## Governance Architecture at the Freeze Date

The architecture by May 23, 2026 was therefore legible. Intrator and Venturo remained founder-executives and directors; McBee remained central to capital formation without holding a board seat; Salanki remained the senior technical co-founder; Agrawal, Jain, Goldberg and O'Rourke formed the newer operating layer; and the board had been thickened with Boone, Hutchins and Whitman. The critical question for investors was not whether CoreWeave had become conventionally governed. It had not. The question was whether this hybrid model — founder control, institutional capital and newly added independent oversight — could manage a business whose backlog was nearing $100 billion and whose debt had already exceeded $21 billion.

chapters.title: Microsoft, OpenAI, hyperscalers, and the Nvidia GPU supply chain
chapters.body:
## The Anchor Relationship

The Microsoft concentration reflected a deliberate strategic choice to pursue multi-year reserved-capacity contracts rather than the spot-market GPU rental model favored by smaller competitors. The March 2025 S-1 said Microsoft accounted for 62 percent of 2024 revenue; the 2025 annual report later said Microsoft accounted for approximately 67 percent of 2025 revenue. Microsoft was not simply a large customer but the anchor that made CoreWeave's financing model legible to lenders. [CoreWeave S-1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525044231/d899798ds1.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm)

The contract structure benefited CoreWeave's balance sheet because committed forward revenue could underwrite GPU procurement and associated debt. It also meant that revenue visibility remained tied to a counterparty that was building its own AI infrastructure at hyperscale. That is why Microsoft remained the persistent investor question even after the company diversified its backlog.

## The OpenAI Dimension

The OpenAI relationship was more concrete, and more fluid, than the IPO-era shorthand suggested. CoreWeave announced an initial OpenAI agreement in March 2025 with contract value up to $11.9 billion, said in May 2025 that the relationship had expanded by another $4 billion, and announced in September 2025 a further agreement worth up to $6.5 billion, taking total announced OpenAI commitments to approximately $22.4 billion. The 2025 10-K and the March 31, 2026 10-Q then described the current master-services-agreement structure more narrowly, saying OpenAI had committed to pay up to approximately $6.5 billion through May 31, 2031 under the September 2025 order form. [CoreWeave Q1 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Q2 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Second-Quarter-2025-Results/) [CoreWeave OpenAI expansion](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Expands-Agreement-with-OpenAI-by-up-to-6-5B/default.aspx) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000222/crwv-20260331.htm)

The important point was not the legal packaging but the strategic implication: OpenAI was no longer merely traffic routed through Microsoft. It had become a direct CoreWeave counterparty as well, giving the company a second AI-lab anchor inside the same wider ecosystem.

## Beyond the Anchors

By the freeze date, the diversification story had broadened materially. The 10-Q showed that the top two customers accounted for 65 percent of first-quarter 2026 revenue, down from a 72 percent share for the top customer alone in the first quarter of 2025. Meta first appeared in the third-quarter 2025 results with a contract worth up to approximately $14.2 billion, then expanded the relationship in April 2026 to about $21 billion through December 2032. Anthropic signed a multi-year agreement on April 10, 2026, and Jane Street announced on April 15, 2026 that it had committed approximately $6 billion to use CoreWeave's cloud platform while also making a $1 billion equity investment. [CoreWeave Q1 2026 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000222/crwv-20260331.htm) [CoreWeave Q3 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Third-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Meta expansion](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-and-Meta-Announce-21-Billion-Expanded-AI-Infrastructure-Agreement/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Anthropic agreement](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Announces-Multi-Year-Agreement-With-Anthropic/default.aspx) [Jane Street agreement](https://www.coreweave.com/news/jane-street-signs-6-billion-ai-cloud-agreement-with-coreweave)

Those additions did not eliminate concentration risk. They did, however, change its shape. The company's question by mid-2026 was no longer whether it could attract customers beyond Microsoft; it was whether those newer counterparties would convert backlog into revenue quickly enough to rebalance the income statement.

## The Nvidia Tripartite

Nvidia occupied three distinct roles at once: principal hardware supplier, strategic investor and contractual backstop participant. The prospectus described a backstop purchase architecture around GPU inventory, while the 2026 proxy showed Nvidia still as a 5 percent-plus holder after the IPO. The relationship mattered because access to the newest Nvidia systems remained one of the central competitive variables in the AI cloud market. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm)

## Infrastructure and Networking

CoreWeave's physical infrastructure remained lease-based rather than land-heavy. The 10-K said the company leased data-center space across the United States, the United Kingdom, Spain, Sweden and Norway, while the AI data-centers page said that, as of December 31, 2025, the platform operated 43 data centers across North America and Europe with 850-plus MW of active power. The May 2026 results release said active power had passed 1 GW and contracted power had exceeded 3.5 GW. [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave AI data centers](https://www.coreweave.com/ai-infrastructure) [CoreWeave Q1 2026 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2026-Results/default.aspx)

On networking, the company marketed high-performance interconnect as part of the platform rather than as a hidden infrastructure layer. Its public documentation described CoreWeave Kubernetes Service as the core managed environment for training and inference, while SUNK provided Slurm on Kubernetes for batch and burst workloads. That combination helped explain why the company sold not only raw GPU capacity, but an operating model for large-scale AI jobs. [CoreWeave platform](https://www.coreweave.com/platform) [CoreWeave docs](https://docs.coreweave.com/docs/platform) [CoreWeave SUNK docs](https://docs.coreweave.com/docs/products/sunk/kubernetes-and-sunk/schedule-kubernetes-pods) [CoreWeave HPC interconnect docs](https://docs.coreweave.com/docs/platform/networking/hpc-interconnect)

chapters.title: Where CoreWeave sits against AWS, Azure, GCP, Lambda, and broader GPU cloud
chapters.body:
## A Market Defined by Infrastructure Velocity

The competitive question around CoreWeave was never whether demand for GPU compute existed. The harder question was whether a specialist provider could keep its edge once the hyperscalers accelerated and once rival AI clouds began offering similar hardware generations. Through the freeze date, CoreWeave's answer remained speed, contractual backlog and platform specialization rather than breadth.

## The Hyperscaler Landscape

Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud all approached AI infrastructure as one product line inside a much broader cloud stack. That gave them balance-sheet depth, integrated sales motions and the ability to bundle storage, networking and managed services in ways a specialist provider could not easily match. It also meant GPU capacity was competing internally for capital against many other priorities. CoreWeave's counter-position was simpler: AI infrastructure was the business, not an adjacent category. [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm)

## The Microsoft Paradox

Azure was CoreWeave's largest customer and also one of its clearest competitors. That paradox was the single most distinctive feature of the company's market position. Microsoft's need for external capacity validated CoreWeave's relevance; Microsoft's scale also made it the most obvious long-term insourcing threat. The same relationship that underwrote CoreWeave's financing model therefore also set the boundary of its strategic risk. [CoreWeave S-1](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525044231/d899798ds1.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm)

## Specialized Competitors

Outside the hyperscalers, the specialist field had become more crowded by 2026. Lambda marketed an AI cloud with on-demand instances, multi-node clusters and private-cloud reservations, including H100, H200 and Blackwell-era systems; its private-cloud documentation described reservations ranging from 1,000 GPUs upward and hyperscale clusters of 2,000 to 64,000 GPUs, but the private company did not publicly disclose revenue or fleet-wide financial metrics through the freeze date. Crusoe marketed an AI cloud built around managed Kubernetes, managed Slurm, optimized RDMA networking and a broader "AI factory" positioning, with public emphasis on infrastructure performance and global data-center reach. Nebius, listed on Nasdaq as NBIS, presented itself in 2026 results materials as an AI cloud company with its own European and US infrastructure footprint and a public-market growth profile separate from the US hyperscalers. [Lambda AI Cloud](https://lambda.ai/welcome/ai-cloud) [Lambda Private Cloud docs](https://docs.lambda.ai/private-cloud) [Crusoe Cloud](https://www.crusoe.ai/cloud) [Nebius FY2025 results](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial-results)

| Company | Type | Public status | What was publicly disclosed through the freeze date |
|---|---|---|---|
| CoreWeave | Specialist AI cloud | Nasdaq: CRWV | $60.7B RPO at Dec. 31, 2025; $99.4B revenue backlog at Mar. 31, 2026 |
| Lambda | Specialist AI cloud | Private | Product and reservation formats; no public revenue or fleet-wide financial disclosure |
| Crusoe | Specialist AI cloud / AI infrastructure | Private | Cloud product architecture and positioning; no public revenue disclosure |
| Nebius | Specialist AI cloud | Nasdaq: NBIS | Public financial reporting and investor materials as a listed AI cloud company |
| AWS / Azure / GCP / OCI | General-purpose cloud with AI capacity | Public parents | GPU capacity sold inside broader cloud platforms |

## Structural Differentiation

CoreWeave's core argument against both the hyperscalers and the specialist peers was infrastructure velocity combined with purpose-built software. The company said in the 10-K that CoreWeave Cloud combined proprietary software and orchestration, advanced infrastructure and managed cloud services. Its public platform and documentation pages framed that software layer around CoreWeave Kubernetes Service, Slurm on Kubernetes and operating tooling built specifically for AI workloads. That combination was meant to make CoreWeave more than a broker of scarce Nvidia hardware. [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave platform](https://www.coreweave.com/platform) [CoreWeave docs](https://docs.coreweave.com/docs/platform) [CoreWeave SUNK docs](https://docs.coreweave.com/docs/products/sunk/kubernetes-and-sunk/schedule-kubernetes-pods)

## Pricing and Market Pressure

The competitive pressure point was not simply hardware availability but the direction of pricing once supply loosened. A specialist provider could move faster and optimize more aggressively around AI workloads; a hyperscaler could spread cost, bundle adjacent services and tolerate thinner standalone economics. CoreWeave's defense by the freeze date was therefore not just faster access to GPUs, but a contracted backlog nearing $100 billion and a claim that customers were buying a vertically integrated AI cloud rather than isolated GPU hours. Whether that distinction remained durable as more rivals added similar hardware was the unresolved question.

chapters.title: From 2017 founding through March 2025 IPO and post-IPO quarters
chapters.body:
## The March 2025 IPO

Shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker CRWV on March 28, 2025 after the company priced the offering the prior evening at $40 per share. The final prospectus showed 37.5 million shares sold, of which 36.59 million came from the company and 910,000 from selling stockholders. That implied roughly $1.46 billion of gross primary proceeds and only about $36.4 million of gross selling-stockholder proceeds; the 2025 annual report later recorded approximately $1.4 billion of net IPO proceeds to the company, plus another $68 million from the partial exercise of the underwriters' over-allotment option in April 2025. [CoreWeave prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000119312525067651/d899798d424b4.htm) [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm)

## Post-IPO Quarters and Forward Catalysts

The post-IPO reporting cycle quickly turned the story from aspiration into measurable execution. Revenue rose from $981.6 million in the first quarter of 2025 to $1.21 billion in the second, $1.36 billion in the third and $1.57 billion in the fourth; revenue backlog moved from $25.9 billion at March 31, 2025 to $30.1 billion at June 30, $55.6 billion at September 30 and $66.8 billion at December 31. By May 7, 2026, CoreWeave reported first-quarter revenue of $2.078 billion and revenue backlog of $99.4 billion. [CoreWeave Q1 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Q2 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Second-Quarter-2025-Results/) [CoreWeave Q3 2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2025/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Third-Quarter-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave FY2025 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-Fourth-Quarter-and-Fiscal-Year-2025-Results/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Q1 2026 results](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-2026-Results/default.aspx)

The customer roster also widened in visible ways after the IPO. CoreWeave said in April 2026 that Meta had expanded its commitment to approximately $21 billion through December 2032; Anthropic signed a multi-year agreement the next day; and Jane Street announced a roughly $6 billion cloud commitment accompanied by a $1 billion equity investment on April 15. Those announcements mattered because they helped convert "diversification" from management rhetoric into named, dated counterparties. [CoreWeave Meta expansion](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-and-Meta-Announce-21-Billion-Expanded-AI-Infrastructure-Agreement/default.aspx) [CoreWeave Anthropic agreement](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Announces-Multi-Year-Agreement-With-Anthropic/default.aspx) [Jane Street agreement](https://www.coreweave.com/news/jane-street-signs-6-billion-ai-cloud-agreement-with-coreweave)

## Capital Structure Dynamics

Capital structure remained a live variable throughout the first year as a public company. Debt principal reached $21.615 billion by December 31, 2025. In March 2026, CoreWeave announced an $8.5 billion financing facility that it described as the first investment-grade-rated GPU-backed financing, and in May 2026 it announced a further $3.1 billion DDTL 5.0 facility. Jane Street's $1 billion equity investment added a different kind of financing signal: not just lender confidence, but willingness by a major customer to put equity on the balance sheet. [CoreWeave 2025 annual report](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000104/crwv-20251231.htm) [CoreWeave $8.5B financing](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Closes-Landmark-8-5-Billion-Financing-Facility-Achieving-First-Investment-Grade-Rated-GPU-backed-Financing/default.aspx) [CoreWeave $3.1B financing](https://investors.coreweave.com/news/news-details/2026/CoreWeave-Closes-3-1-Billion-Loan-Facility-Expanding-Access-to-Public-Markets-for-GPU-backed-Financing/default.aspx) [Jane Street agreement](https://www.coreweave.com/news/jane-street-signs-6-billion-ai-cloud-agreement-with-coreweave)

## Governance Continuity

The co-founder operating team remained intact through the initial public-company period, but the governance picture was more formalized by the freeze date than it had been at listing. The April 2026 proxy showed a six-member board comprising Intrator, Venturo, Karen Boone, Glenn Hutchins, Margaret Whitman and Jack Cogen, with Hutchins serving as Lead Independent Director and Cogen already having notified the board that he would not stand for re-election at the June annual meeting. [CoreWeave 2026 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000191/crwv-20260422.htm)
